title: You Come From This
author: The Daily Stoic
summary: This Daily Stoic meditation takes on the modern suspicion that comfortable people must be soft by comparison with the Greeks, the Romans or their own grandparents. Drawing on David McCullough's History Matters, it concedes that earlier generations endured hardships but reframes the comparison: every generation, including Marcus Aurelius relative to Zeno, lived in what was then the most advanced moment in history and still met crises when they came. The move is to replace nostalgia and self-doubt with a sense of inheritance, so that the reader locates themselves in a lineage of people who survived wars, depressions and famines. It then reminds the reader that they have already weathered pandemics, political unrest and personal trouble. The closing line, borrowed from Churchill via McCullough, is that we are not made of sugar candy. The piece is short and exhortatory, a resilience reflection framed around historical continuity.
points: The piece rejects the assumption that modern comfort makes people weaker than their ancestors or the ancient Stoics.
Its central observation is that every era, including Marcus Aurelius's, was the most advanced age its people had yet known.
It borrows Churchill's line, via David McCullough, that we have not journeyed this far because we are made of sugar candy.
Resilience is framed as an inheritance from ancestors who endured wars, depressions, famines and floods.
quotes: You have it pretty good. We all do. You have modern conveniences. You live in a time of relative peace.
So it is easy to get a little spoiled…it’s also easy to assume that you are spoiled and soft. Especially compared to the ancient Greeks and Romans, or even our own ancestors.
Your ancestors also lived in what was then a relatively advanced time—in the most advanced time in human history…up until that point.
Marcus Aurelius had conveniences Zeno did not, just as your ancestors 80 years ago had things that even an ancient king did not.
You come from that tradition. You are made from the same stock as the Stoics. You are literally from the stock of the people who lived through wars and depressions and famines and floods.
You yourself, it should be pointed out, have been through some stuff—pandemics and panics, political unrest and personal issues. You are not made of sugar candy. You can handle this.
